title: Spanish Punctuation Rules: ¿ ¡, Commas, Quotes and Dashes
seo_title: Spanish Punctuation Rules: ¿ ¡, Commas, Quotes and Dashes
meta_description: Spanish punctuation rules for learners: opening ¿ and ¡, commas, decimal commas, « » quotes, the dialogue dash and periods, with mistakes and a quiz.
excerpt: Upside-down question marks are only the beginning.
body_html:
Spanish punctuation rules are mostly familiar to learners, with a few important differences. The famous one is the opening question and exclamation mark: ¿Cómo estás?, ¡Qué bien!. But there are others that matter in emails, essays and anything you publish: where the period goes with quotes, which quotation marks to use, how dialogue is punctuated in novels, and why some countries write 3,5 instead of 3.5. Here’s a practical guide.

Key takeaways
  • Questions and exclamations open with ¿ and ¡, exactly where they begin.
  • No Oxford comma before y: pan, leche y huevos.
  • Spanish prefers « » quotes, then “ ”, then ‘ ’; the period goes after the closing quote.
  • Dialogue in books uses the long dash (—), not quotation marks.
{{toc}}

Spanish punctuation rules for ¿ and ¡

Spanish marks the beginning of a question or exclamation, so the reader knows the intonation from the start. The Real Academia Española treats both opening signs as obligatory in standard writing.

  • ¿Dónde vives? Where do you live?
  • ¡Feliz cumpleaños! Happy birthday!

Mid-sentence questions

The opening sign goes where the question actually starts, not at the start of the sentence:

  • Si no vienes, ¿me llamas? If you’re not coming, will you call me?
  • Ana, ¿tienes un momento? Ana, do you have a moment?
  • Es bonito, ¿verdad? It’s pretty, isn’t it?

Lower case continues after the opening sign if the question is in the middle: Oye, ¿vienes? No space goes after ¿ or before ?.

Combining both

For a surprised question, you can mix them: ¿¡Qué has hecho!? or ¡¿Qué has hecho?!. Doubling or tripling signs (¡¡¡Hola!!!) is acceptable only in very informal writing.

Commas

No Oxford comma

Spanish doesn’t put a comma before y, o or ni in a simple list: Compré pan, leche y huevos.

Vocative comma

Always separate the name of the person you address: Hola, María. / Gracias, mamá. Without it, Vamos a comer niños means something rather different from Vamos a comer, niños.

No comma between subject and verb

A common error is Mi hermano y yo, vamos a Madrid. Correct: Mi hermano y yo vamos a Madrid.

{{image:2}}

Numbers: decimals and thousands

In Spain, Argentina, Chile and many other countries, the decimal separator is a comma: 3,5 kilos. In Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean, it is a point: 3.5 kilos. The RAE now recommends a thin space, not a point, for thousands in numbers of five digits or more: 10 000, 1 500 000; four-digit numbers are written together: 2026, 1500.

Quotation marks

Spanish style recommends angled quotes first, then English-style quotes inside them, then single quotes:

Me dijo: «Lo llamaron “el genio” en el colegio».

In practice, many websites and Latin American publications use “ ” as the main quotation marks, which is also acceptable. One firm rule: the period goes after the closing quote or parenthesis: «Ya voy»., not «Ya voy.»

{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

The dialogue dash

Spanish novels and stories mark dialogue with the long dash (raya), not quotation marks:

—¿Vienes? —preguntó Lucía.
—Ahora mismo —respondí.

The dash opens each line of speech, and a second dash introduces the narrator’s comment. If you read bilingual books, you’ll see this difference on every page; it’s one of the things I always adapt when translating fiction. See {{link:parallel-text-reading|parallel text reading}}.

Other differences

  • Letters and emails: the greeting ends with a colon, not a comma: Estimada Sra. López:. See {{link:writing-emails-in-spanish|writing emails in Spanish}}.
  • Ellipsis: exactly three dots, no space before: Pues…
  • Abbreviations: Sr., Dra., etc., and the period is not doubled at the end of a sentence.
  • Capital letters after a colon: usually lower case, except after the greeting of a letter. See {{link:spanish-capitalization-rules|Spanish capitalization rules}}.

Why this matters

Missing opening question marks are the most visible punctuation error learners make, and in texting many natives skip them too. In formal writing, though, they are expected, and so are the other conventions above. As a translator, punctuation is one of the final checks I run on every text, because English punctuation habits carried into Spanish make a translation look unfinished even when the words are perfect.

Try it yourself

Punctuate correctly: oye tienes tiempo mañana / hola pedro que tal / compré manzanas peras y uvas

Answers: Oye, ¿tienes tiempo mañana? / Hola, Pedro, ¿qué tal? / Compré manzanas, peras y uvas.

Accents are covered in {{link:spanish-accent-marks|Spanish accent marks}}, and all mistake types in {{link:common-spanish-mistakes|my guide to common Spanish mistakes}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Open your questions and exclamations, drop the Oxford comma, add the vocative comma, put the period after quotes, and recognize the dialogue dash when you read. With those habits, your written Spanish will look as good as it sounds.

faq.q: Why does Spanish use upside-down question marks?
faq.a: To show where a question or exclamation begins, so the reader knows the intonation from the start. The RAE considers them obligatory.

faq.q: Where does the opening question mark go in a long sentence?
faq.a: Where the question itself starts: Si no puedes venir, ¿me avisas?

faq.q: Does Spanish use the Oxford comma?
faq.a: No. Spanish does not put a comma before y in a simple list: pan, leche y huevos.

questions.explain: The opening sign goes where the question starts.
